title: After a sin
hook: all children of Adam err, and the best of them repent (Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: how did a father wait for a son he thought was gone?

segments.voice: Yesterday, when you fail: two sentences. Allah decreed it, and the next step is still yours. Today, a different kind of failing: the one that landed on someone.
screen: `WHEN YOU FAIL: TWO SENTENCES.` → `NOW, THE ONE THAT LANDED.`

segments.voice: The thing said in the kitchen, in a voice you'd never use on a stranger, to the person who'd do anything for you. Then the second hard part, which can be worse: the replay, the shame, the urge to avoid her eyes for a week. So what does anyone do after doing wrong? It's one of the oldest questions people ask, and this tradition's answer starts with a family name.
screen: `THE THING SAID IN THE KITCHEN.` → `THEN THE SHAME.` → `WHAT DOES ANYONE DO NEXT?`

segments.voice: The Prophet ﷺ put it plainly, in Tirmidhi: every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who repent. Not the ones who never fall; that list is empty. The best are the ones who come back. It runs in the family. In the Qur'an, Adam and his wife eat from the tree, and their first words afterward aren't excuses: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!" Name it, own it, turn back. And the door stays wide: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." When the wrong landed on a person, there's a second door. The Prophet said whoever has wronged someone should make it right with them today. So tawba after a cruel word runs two ways: to God, and to her. Here's something shared with a neighbor. The Hebrew Bible says it too, in an older Jewish translation: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." Jewish tradition calls the way back teshuvah, return, and the Mishnah teaches that a wrong against another person waits on that person's forgiveness too. One honest difference: Jewish tradition also gives return a season each year, the Days of Awe, ending in Yom Kippur, prayed together as a congregation. The hadith names no season; its door is open on any ordinary night.
screen: `EVERY CHILD OF ADAM ERRS.` · `WE HAVE WRONGED OURSELVES.` · `TWO DOORS: TO GOD, AND TO HER.` · `TESHUVAH: A NEIGHBOR'S RETURN.` · then, large: `THE BEST RETURN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring back one wrong that's still sitting with you. Don't replay the scene; just name it plainly, the way Adam did. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, slowly, a few times; if not, breathe with the name of it. Before you open your eyes, picture the first small step toward the person, if there is one.
screen: `NAME IT, DON'T REPLAY IT.` · `ASTAGHFIRULLAH, SLOWLY.` · `ONE STEP TOWARD THEM.`

segments.voice: After a sin: every child of Adam errs. The best of them return, to God, and to whoever they hurt.
Hold onto this: the best return, for every child of Adam who falls. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1728 COUNTS.` → `HARD DAYS · 7 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DID A FATHER WAIT FOR A LOST SON?`

howItsDone: Muslims repent (tawba) by stopping the wrong, regretting it, resolving not to return to it and asking Allah's forgiveness, often saying astaghfirullah; when a person was wronged, they also seek that person's pardon and set things right.

chat.meaning: The best who err are those who repent. When the wrong landed on a person, the way back includes making it right with them, not only with God.
